Case 04 — Disney (DIS): license the library, or withhold it?

3 min read666 wordsUpdated 2026-10-19acumen/case-04-disney.md
On this page
  1. The brief
  2. Pull the real data
  3. Canon to bring to bear
  4. Your deliverable — the 1-page board memo
  5. YOUR MEMO
  6. RED-TEAM (after you submit)

Status: OPEN — awaiting your memo. Rep type: strategic choice cascade + coopetition + commitment. Size: full (~90 min) — see the menu in MECHANISM.md. No answer key. This one is genuinely contested inside the industry. Take a side.

The brief

Disney spent the streaming era pulling its library back from rivals to feed its own service, on the theory that exclusivity is the moat. The strategy has a cost: content that once earned high-margin licensing revenue from a competitor now earns nothing directly, while the direct-to-consumer business absorbs the marketing and churn expense of holding the same subscriber.

Meanwhile the industry has partially reversed: several studios resumed licensing selected titles to the largest aggregator, arguing that the library earns more as a rented asset than as a retention tool, and that windowing beats withholding. Disney sits on the most valuable library and the strongest brand franchises, which makes the question sharper rather than easier — it has the most to gain from licensing and the most to lose from training audiences to find its content elsewhere.

Verify before you reason. Confirm the current state of Disney's licensing posture, its DTC segment profitability, and its content spend — from the filings, not from this brief or from memory.

The decision: Over the next three years, should Disney license a defined tier of its library to rival platforms (and if so, which tier and on what terms), or hold exclusivity and accept lower near-term content monetisation — and what is the single thing that, if wrong, sinks your plan?

Pull the real data

python3 _ingest/edgar.py company DIS
python3 _ingest/edgar.py filings DIS --form 10-K     # segment results; Item 1A; content spend
python3 _ingest/edgar.py facts DIS                   # segment revenue/OI, capitalised content, FCF
python3 _ingest/edgar.py search "content licensing"  # how peers describe the same trade

Anchor the call in: DTC segment operating income and its trajectory, content spend, and the licensing/other revenue line. Compare against at least one peer that chose the opposite policy — the counterfactual is doing the analytical work here.

Canon to bring to bear

canon-lafley-martin-playing-to-win (the cascade: where to play, how to win — and what you won't do) · canon-brandenburger-nalebuff-coopetition (a rival can be a complementor; the value net, not the battlefield) · canon-schelling-strategy-of-conflict (a commitment only works if it is credible and visible; exclusivity is a commitment) · canon-helmer-7-powers (if you can't name the barrier, you don't have a moat — which of the seven is actually operating here?)

Four frameworks. If you need a fifth, you have widened the question. Anything you reach for that is not on this list is exactly what the meta-question is hunting for.

Your deliverable — the 1-page board memo

To the spec in README.md:

  1. Recommendation (BLUF) — the call, one sentence. Not "a hybrid approach."
  2. The crux — the pivotal, solvable challenge it turns on.
  3. Why — three reasons, each with a real figure from the filings.
  4. The fatal risk + mitigation — the one thing that, if wrong, sinks it.
  5. The ask — what you want the board to approve.

Attach a forecast. One falsifiable statement with a probability and a resolution date.

Two traps this case is built to catch. First, "license the non-franchise tail and keep the franchises" is the obvious answer — if that is your call, the memo has to defend where the line sits and why that line is defensible, or it is a tradeoffs matrix wearing a recommendation's clothes. Second, naming exclusivity as the moat without naming which of Helmer's seven powers it actually is scores badly on Evidence.
